1.q: וַ⁠יְהִי֩ כְּ⁠כַלּ֨וֹת יִרְמְיָ֜הוּ לְ⁠דַבֵּ֣ר אֶל כָּל הָ⁠עָ֗ם
1.note: Jeremiah is using the phrase translated as **And it happened** to introduce a new event in the story. Use a word, phrase, or other method in your language that is natural for introducing a new event.

1.q: אֶת כָּל דִּבְרֵי֙ יְהוָ֣ה אֱלֹהֵי⁠הֶ֔ם & אֵ֥ת כָּל הַ⁠דְּבָרִ֖ים הָ⁠אֵֽלֶּה
1.note: It might seem that the expression **all these words** contains extra information that would not be natural to express in your language, since it repeats the idea of **all the words of Yahweh their God** earlier in the verse. If so, you could shorten it or adjust it. Alternate translation: [all the words of Yahweh their God … every one of them]

2.q: עֲזַרְיָ֤ה בֶן הוֹשַֽׁעְיָה֙ וְ⁠יוֹחָנָ֣ן בֶּן קָרֵ֔חַ
2.note: The words **Azariah**, **Hoshaiah**, **Johanan**, and **Kareah** are the names of men.
If your language does not use a noun for the idea of **Falsehood**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [You are speaking what is not true]

2.q: לֹ֣א שְׁלָחֲ⁠ךָ֞ יְהוָ֤ה אֱלֹהֵ֨י⁠נוּ֙ לֵ⁠אמֹ֔ר לֹֽא תָבֹ֥אוּ מִצְרַ֖יִם לָ⁠ג֥וּר שָֽׁם
2.note: If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. Alternate translation: [Yahweh our God did not send you to say that we should not go to Egypt to sojourn there]
See how you translated the similar expression in 35:12.

3.note: See how you translated the names **Baruch** and **Neriah** in 32:12.

By **us**, Azariah, Johanan, and the men with them mean themselves and the people with them but not Jeremiah, to whom they are speaking, so use the exclusive form of that word in your translation if your language marks that distinction.
See how you translated the similar expression in 22:25.

4.note: See how you translated the similar phrase “to my voice you did not listen” in 3:13. Alternate translation: [And … did not obey what Yahweh had said]

5.note: The expression **had been driven** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you must say who did the action, the context indicates that their enemies did it. Alternate translation: [where their enemies had driven them]

6.note: Jeremiah is using the term **soul** to mean the entire person from the perspective of his spiritual/emotional existence. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [every person]

6.q: אֲשֶׁ֤ר הִנִּ֨יחַ֙ נְבוּזַרְאֲדָ֣ן רַב טַבָּחִ֔ים אֶת גְּדַלְיָ֖הוּ בֶּן אֲחִיקָ֣ם בֶּן שָׁפָ֑ן
6.note: The words **Nebuzaradan**, **Gedaliah**, **Ahikam**, and **Shaphan** are the names of men.

7.note: See how you translated “did not listen to the voice of Yahweh” in 43:4.
The word **Tahpanhes** is the name of a city in Egypt.

8.note: See how you translated the similar expression in 28:12.

9.q: קַ֣ח בְּ⁠יָדְ⁠ךָ֞ אֲבָנִ֣ים גְּדֹל֗וֹת וּ⁠טְמַנְתָּ֤⁠ם בַּ⁠מֶּ֨לֶט֙ בַּ⁠מַּלְבֵּ֔ן
9.note: Burying large stones in the pavement at the entrance of the royal building was a symbolic action by which Jeremiah showed that the king of Babylon would come and set up his throne in that very place in order to rule over Egypt. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explain the significance of this action in the text of your translation or in a footnote. Alternate translation: [As a sign that the king of Babylon will come and set up his throne at this place, take in your hand large stones, and you shall hide them in the mortar in the brick pavement]

The **mortar** is a kind of wet clay that people used to hold bricks or stones together, and a **brick pavement** is a kind of floor or courtyard made of bricks. If your readers would not be familiar with what these are, you could use the names of similar things that your readers would recognize, or you could use more general terms. Alternate translation: [in the clay under the bricks of the courtyard floor]
See how you translated the similar expression in 19:10.
The word **Tahpanhes** is the name of a city in Egypt.

10.q: וְ⁠אָמַרְתָּ֣ אֲלֵי⁠הֶ֡ם כֹּֽה אָמַר֩ יְהוָ֨ה צְבָא֜וֹת אֱלֹהֵ֣י יִשְׂרָאֵ֗ל
10.note: See how you translated the similar expression in 25:27.
See how you translated this phrase in 25:9.

Yahweh is speaking of Nebuchadnezzar as if he were Yahweh’s **servant**. He means that he will use Nebuchadnezzar to accomplish what he wants, even though Nebuchadnezzar does not worship Yahweh. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a comparable expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, whom I will use to accomplish my purposes]

Setting a throne up was a symbolic action which showed that Nebuchadnezzar would rule over Egypt. In that culture when a king conquered an enemies’ kingdom they would set up a portable throne at the city gate to hold court and accept surrender. Here Nebuchadnezzar sets up his thrown at the doorstep or entrance to Pharaoh’s palace. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explain the significance of this action in the text of your translation as in the UST or you could put the information in a footnote.

A **canopy** is a kind of large tent or covering that a king would set up over his throne. If your readers would not be familiar with what a canopy is, you could use the name of a similar thing that your readers would recognize, or you could use a more general term. Alternate translation: [and he will spread out his royal covering over them]

11.note: Here, **the land of Egypt** represents “the people who live in the land of Egypt,” and **strike** means “attack.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [And he will come and attack the people who live in Egypt]

11.q: אֲשֶׁ֧ר לַ⁠מָּ֣וֶת לַ⁠מָּ֗וֶת וַ⁠אֲשֶׁ֤ר לַ⁠שְּׁבִי֙ לַ⁠שֶּׁ֔בִי וַ⁠אֲשֶׁ֥ר לַ⁠חֶ֖רֶב לֶ⁠חָֽרֶב
11.note: Yahweh is using the expressions **for death, to death**, **for captivity, to captivity**, and **for the sword, to the sword** as common expressions of the culture to mean “each person will die from disease, be taken captive, or be killed in battle, as Yahweh has decided for him.” If these phrases do not have that meaning for your readers, you could use comparable expressions from your language that do have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [those whom I have destined to die of disease will die of disease; those whom I have destined to be captured will be captured; and those whom I have destined to die in battle will die in battle]

12.note: The standard written Hebrew text as we have it today reads “**And I will kindle**.” The ULT follows that reading. In this reading the “I” refers to Yahweh. Other ancient manuscripts read “And he will kindle.” In this reading the “he” refers to Nebuchadnezzar. This is the reading followed by the UST (which reflects Nebuchadnezzar’s soldiers kindling a fire at his command). The UST reflect the “he will kindle” reading because this is the most probable reading in context since the previous verse uses “he” multiple times (referring to Nebuchadnezzar doing the actions) and the rest of this verse uses “he” (referring to Nebuchadnezzar doing the actions). If a translation of the Bible exists in your region, you may wish to use the reading that it uses. If a translation of the Bible does not exist in your region, you may wish to use the reading of the UST.

Jeremiah assumes that readers will know that the Egyptians worshiped idols in temples, and that these idols were thought of as gods, though they were not real gods. You could say that explicitly if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [in the temples of the false gods that the Egyptians worship] or [in the temples of the idols of Egypt]

The pronoun **he** refers to Nebuchadnezzar, not to Yahweh, who is speaking. The first **them** refers to the houses (temples) of the gods, and the second **them** refers to the gods themselves, that is, the idols. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [and Nebuchadnezzar will burn those houses and take those idols captive] or [and Nebuchadnezzar will burn those temples and take those idols as plunder]

12.q: וְ⁠עָטָה֩ אֶת אֶ֨רֶץ מִצְרַ֜יִם כַּ⁠אֲשֶׁר יַעְטֶ֤ה הָֽ⁠רֹעֶה֙ אֶת בִּגְד֔⁠וֹ
12.note: The point of this comparison is that just as **the shepherd wraps himself** with **his garment** easily and completely, so Nebuchadnezzar will take control of all of **the land of Egypt** easily and completely. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [And he will take control of all the land of Egypt as easily as a shepherd wraps himself with his garment]

Yahweh is using **he will go out from there in peace** as a common expression of the culture to mean “he will leave there safely, without anyone harming him.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and he will leave there unharmed]
If your language does not use a noun for the idea of **peace**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [safely]

13.q: אֶֽת מַצְּבוֹת֙ בֵּ֣ית שֶׁ֔מֶשׁ אֲשֶׁ֖ר בְּ⁠אֶ֣רֶץ מִצְרָ֑יִם
13.note: The words **Beth Shemesh** are the name of a city in Egypt. This is not the town in Judah that has the same name. The word **Beth** means “house” and the word **Shemesh** means “sun” so the phrase **Beth Shemesh** means “house of the sun” or “temple of the sun.” You may want to include that information in a footnote.

13.q: וְ⁠אֶת בָּתֵּ֥י אֱלֹהֵֽי מִצְרַ֖יִם יִשְׂרֹ֥ף בָּ⁠אֵֽשׁ
13.note: If it would be more natural in your language, you may want to put the information about burning before the information about **the houses of the gods of Egypt**. Alternate translation: [and he will burn the houses of the gods of Egypt with fire]
See how you translated “the houses of the gods of Egypt” in the previous verse.
See how you translated the similar expression in 21:10.
